<reason>A anchored its case to the motion as written: the contrast is opt-in consent versus broad "all media hereafter devised" boilerplate, and A repeatedly showed B never defended that boilerplate, while every protection B offered (disclosed, specific, negotiated terms) sits on A's side of the line. A's necessary-vs-sufficient pivot converted B's main attack into an apparent concession, and A2.5 cleanly dismantled B's "already licensed performance" framing, which B never rebuilt. B landed real blows — the porous-where-needed/rigid-where-not asymmetry and especially the non-response problem, which A answered only thinly and late (and with a borderline-new "registries/proxies" fix in closing). But B's claim that union-specified consent dissolves the motion strained against the motion's actual wording, its case drifted toward "opt-in is insufficient" rather than "opt-in should not be required," and its clipped Rebuttal 2 was a real execution cost. A made the debate easier to decide on the proposition's own terms.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A2.5's inversion of the 80-year dubbing analogy (traditional dubbing hired a new paid performer; AI extracts the original's identity — "the taking is new; the license is old") killed B's no-taking frame, after which A4.5–4.6's "consent is necessary, not sufficient — your best argument is that it needs a partner" sequence reframed B's entire case as concession; B's partial recovery via the non-response point kept it competitive.</best_rebuttal>
